prize_parts.citation: for incorporating firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, showing how exporter selection and reallocation across firms shape the gains from trade.

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single part on firm heterogeneity and selection, credited to Melitz and Helpman. The substantive case is this. Melitz (2003) made the heterogeneous firm the unit of analysis. That produced selection into exporting and reallocation across firms as new channels for gains from trade, and it explained facts such as exporter premia and the productivity effects of liberalisation. It also gave the large literature built on firm-level customs and administrative data a shared theoretical language. The framework is more than twenty years old, is standard in teaching and policy evaluation, and has been confronted with firm-level data from many countries. The central qualitative claim, that selection and reallocation matter for aggregate productivity, has held up even though welfare magnitudes remain debated. The chair asked whether Helpman is the right second name. My answer is yes, for the work on this ballot entry. Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple extended the framework to the exporting-versus-FDI choice, and his wider heterogeneous-firm agenda helped make it a research programme and not a single paper. I would write the citation around the theoretical framework and not claim to honour all firm-level trade research. This case rests on the evidence record and on whether the credit can be identified. It does not rest on how many colleagues listed B026. Cleaner attribution is only a practical advantage and I do not count it as merit.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution at the edges. Bernard and Jensen established the exporter-premium facts that the theory later explained, and Eaton and Kortum built a parallel quantitative line. Neither is a credited name on this ballot entry, so a Melitz-Helpman prize could be read as under-crediting them. The Committee can credit only shortlisted names, so that omission cannot be repaired within this configuration. I treat it as a real cost and not as a technicality. Helpman's wider record is also spread across other strands, including trade politics, so his place here rests on the heterogeneous-firm work alone. The overlap with the 2008 prize on new trade theory is arguable. I think the discoveries are distinct, but I cannot settle that from the written record. Welfare calculations depend on functional-form assumptions such as the productivity distribution. If the Committee finds the Bernard-Jensen and Eaton-Kortum omissions too serious, waiting is a defensible position.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B007 first and B026 second. He agrees Melitz (2003) is the anchor and Redding's work is an extension, but says the Committee would have to explain why Helpman is the second name when the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum line is not credited. He prefers B007 because its two-author credit has no obvious missing claimant.
responses.response: That is the strongest form of the attribution objection, and I accept the omissions as a cost. I would explain Helpman's place as follows. The discovery is the theoretical framework of heterogeneity and selection, and Helpman is the co-author who carried it into exporting versus FDI and into a wider research agenda. Bernard and Jensen's exporter facts are what the framework explains, and Eaton-Kortum answers a different, Ricardian and quantitative question, so neither is a rival claimant to the framework itself. I also note that B007 is not free of the problem. Its pair has no uncredited claimant, but its mechanism is less cleanly identified empirically, and you concede that point. A missing empirical co-pioneer does not undo a discovery that has been tested this widely. I treat your preference for B007 as a considered judgment and keep it as my second alternative.

responses.point: Strömberg proposes a two-part prize: Kiyotaki and Moore (B007) and Melitz alone (B026). He says he would prefer to name Helpman, and that he would support Melitz and Helpman if B026 stood alone.
responses.response: I take your answer to the chair's question as the most useful information on B026 so far. You would back the pair if B026 stood alone. I do not support the two-part version, for three reasons. First, it names only Melitz, so the cap decides the attribution and the evidence does not. You say the same about your own proposal. Second, no other member has proposed combining the parts, and the Committee has not tested whether B007 and B026 supporters would accept a combination. Third, combining macro-finance with trade has no thematic reason and looks like an arithmetic product of the three-person limit. I would not exclude a two-part prize on principle. I would want it to follow from the substance of two achievements, and not from the need to find a majority.

responses.point: Enflo prefers B009 with Persson, Tabellini and Besley, and keeps B026 as an alternative. She argues that B009 differs from the 2024 institutions prize because it explains within-polity policy formation. She would keep Besley because Persson links the constitutions strand and the state-capacity strand.
responses.response: Your distinction from the 2024 prize is a fair one, and it has softened my adjacency worry. Colonial-origin institutions and long-run prosperity are a different question from why electoral rules produce different fiscal outcomes. I also agree that Persson connecting both strands is a good reason for the three-name structure. Two things keep me from ranking B009 above B026. The first is the evidence base. The theory and the later state-capacity work are persuasive, but some cross-country constitutional estimates rely on weaker identification than the firm-level trade evidence. You concede part of that yourself. The second is that adjacency to a very recent prize is a further cost for B009. I now list B009 below B012 and B007 as an alternative, but I do not dismiss it. Your point that support from members near the field should not be read as agreement on merit applies to me as well. I weigh B026 on the testing record and not on how many colleagues rank it.

responses.point: Krusell now prefers the Kiyotaki-Moore pair, with B026 and B012 as alternatives. He calls B026 a strong case. He says it is better on breadth of influence if the Committee judges that Melitz's originating role makes the pair sufficiently clear.
responses.response: I agree with that conditional, and I think it is the right way to frame the choice between B007 and B026. The conditional is that Melitz's originating role makes the pair clear enough. My reading is that it does. Melitz (2003) is the originating model, and Helpman's work with Melitz on the extensive margin of exporting versus investing abroad builds directly on it. I also accept your point that credit for Helpman is spread across other strands. I would limit the citation to the heterogeneous-firm framework so that the credit is claimed only for what this ballot entry supports. Your move from a three-name to a two-name B007 for attribution reasons is the same kind of discipline I apply to B026.

responses.point: Hassler, the chair, prefers B012. He accepts that B026 is distinct from the 2008 prize and says it is a stronger alternative than he weighted at opening. His remaining reservation is that Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum are not credited and that Helpman also appears under the trade-politics entry.
responses.response: I am glad the distinctness argument holds for you. On your two attribution concerns, I do not think they are resolved, but they are bounded. Eaton-Kortum answers a different question from selection and reallocation, as Fredriksson argued. For Helpman, the citation can rest only on the heterogeneous-firm work, so his trade-politics record does not enter. I also take your point against my own position. B012 has the largest policy footprint on the shortlist, and your argument that Calvo, Taylor and Woodford are separable originators makes its attribution problem more manageable than I credited in round 1. That is why B012 moves to the top of my alternatives. I still find B026's credit more compact, and its evidence record is a more direct test of its central claim than B012's post-2008 and post-2021 record.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee judges that the omission of Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum makes a Melitz-Helpman pair premature or merely incomplete.
Whether the firm-heterogeneity advance is distinct enough from the new trade theory recognised in 2008. I find the argument persuasive but cannot settle it from the written record.
How sensitive the welfare and gains-from-trade magnitudes are to functional-form assumptions, which could weaken the quantitative message more than the qualitative selection result.

Whether a prize for B012 would settle its attribution if the Committee fixed the trio around separable originators (Calvo, Taylor, Woodford), in which case its breadth of influence could outweigh B026's compact credit.
Whether Redding's quantitative and spatial work should be credited. I treat it as a development of the framework, but that is itself an attribution call.
I have not independently verified citation counts, priority claims or the details of the credited authors' contributions.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict is apparent from the supplied profile for B026, B012 or B007. My research is in labour economics and the economics of crime, and my listed frequent co-authors (Bayer, Anwar, Lindquist, Holmlund, Lochner, Bindler) do not appear among the credited names on any shortlisted ballot entry. Nothing in my profile ties me to Melitz, Helpman or any other candidate in my preferred configuration or alternatives. I am a co-opted member, and the profile does not document my relationships with other members beyond the committee. My field is not close to B026, but I note that my interest in firm-level administrative data and in data-driven validation could shape what I value. I disclose these points and do not adjudicate them.
